## Introduction & background

Real-world op-amps do not have infinite speed or infinite bandwidth. The Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBW) is a constant value; if you demand a high voltage gain, your maximum usable frequency drops proportionally. When the input frequency exceeds this limit, the output amplitude simply degrades (the -3 dB point). Completely separate from GBW is Slew Rate (SR), which defines the absolute maximum physical speed (measured in Volts per microsecond) at which the op-amp's output can physically change. Exceeding the bandwidth makes the signal smaller; exceeding the slew rate distorts the signal entirely, turning fast square waves into slow triangles.

## Core equations

Gain-Bandwidth Product:
$$GBW = A_v \cdot f_{-3dB}$$

Slew Rate limit for a sine wave:
$$SR \ge 2\pi f V_{peak}$$

[Texas Instruments: Non-Inverting Amplifier Slew Rate and Bandwidth Constraints (PDF)](https://www.ti.com/lit/sboa271)

## What you're building

1. A non-inverting amplifier wired for a massive ×100 gain using an LM358.
2. A frequency sweep setup to experimentally locate the -3 dB bandwidth drop and calculate the physical Gain-Bandwidth Product.
3. A unity-gain buffer circuit fed with a fast 5 Vpp, 50 kHz square wave.
4. A slew-rate measurement setup utilizing the oscilloscope cursors to calculate the exact slope of the output ramp in $V/\mu s$.
5. A comparative test reproducing both measurements with a TL072 to observe the difference between a standard BJT op-amp and a faster JFET op-amp.

## Activity

Non-inverting ×100 with the LM358: raise input frequency until the output falls to ~70% — that f × 100 = your measured GBW; compare to the datasheet (~1 MHz). Then unity buffer, 5 Vpp 50 kHz square wave in: measure the output ramp slope = slew rate; compare (~0.5 V/µs). Repeat both with the TL072.

## Question to answer

1. For your fast square wave test, which specific limitation distorted it first — bandwidth or slew rate?
2. How do you visually tell the difference between bandwidth limitation and slew-rate limitation on an oscilloscope trace?
